claim: Individuals with congenital amusia have a lifelong history of unreliable pitch processing.
source: Individuals with congenital amusia have a lifelong history of unreliable pitch processing.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about amusia that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Individuals with congenital amusia downweight pitch cues during speech perception and instead rely on other dimensions such as duration.
source: Accordingly, they downweight pitch cues during speech perception and instead rely on other dimensions such as duration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Jasmin et al., 2020a) mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Prominent reductions in functional connectivity were detected in the amusia group between left prefrontal language-related regions and right hemisphere pitch-related regions.
source: Prominent reductions in functional connectivity were detected in the amusia group between left prefrontal language-related regions and right hemisphere pitch-related regions, which reflected the between-group differences in cue weights in the same groups of listeners.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Connectivity differences between left prefrontal language-related regions and right hemisphere pitch-related regions reflected the between-group differences in cue weights.
source: Prominent reductions in functional connectivity were detected in the amusia group between left prefrontal language-related regions and right hemisphere pitch-related regions, which reflected the between-group differences in cue weights in the same groups of listeners.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between functional connectivity and behavioral cue weights presented in the Results section.

claim: Connectivity differences between left prefrontal language-related regions and right hemisphere pitch-related regions were not present during a control task.
source: Connectivity differences between these regions were not present during a control task.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis with passive tone listening data presented in the Results section.

claim: The reliability of perceptual dimensions is linked with functional connectivity between frontal and perceptual regions.
source: Our results indicate that the reliability of perceptual dimensions is linked with functional connectivity between frontal and perceptual regions and suggest a compensatory mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings combining behavioral and neuroimaging data.

claim: The neural findings suggest a compensatory mechanism in individuals with amusia.
source: Our results indicate that the reliability of perceptual dimensions is linked with functional connectivity between frontal and perceptual regions and suggest a compensatory mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data regarding the functional significance of the connectivity differences.

claim: Congenital amusia is a rare condition characterized by impaired perception of and memory for pitch.
source: Congenital amusia is a rare condition characterized by impaired perception of and memory for pitch (Peretz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation to foundational work in the field.

claim: Auditory cortical responses are normal in individuals with congenital amusia.
source: Although congenital amusia presents as an auditory condition, auditory cortical responses are normal (Moreau et al., 2013; Norman-Haignere et al., 2016), as is subcortical encoding of pitch (Liu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Subcortical encoding of pitch is normal in individuals with congenital amusia.
source: Although congenital amusia presents as an auditory condition, auditory cortical responses are normal (Moreau et al., 2013; Norman-Haignere et al., 2016), as is subcortical encoding of pitch (Liu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on brainstem responses.

claim: The dominant view of amusia's neural basis is that connectivity between right inferior frontal cortex and right auditory cortex is impaired.
source: The dominant view of amusia's neural basis is that connectivity between right inferior frontal cortex and right auditory cortex is impaired, resulting in impaired conscious access to pitch information for guiding behavior (Hyde et al., 2011; Albouy et al., 2013; Leveque et al., 2016; Zendel et al., 2015; see Peretz, 2016 for review).
evidence: This claim summarizes the prevailing theoretical account in the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Impaired connectivity between right inferior frontal cortex and right auditory cortex results in impaired conscious access to pitch information for guiding behavior.
source: The dominant view of amusia's neural basis is that connectivity between right inferior frontal cortex and right auditory cortex is impaired, resulting in impaired conscious access to pitch information for guiding behavior (Hyde et al., 2011; Albouy et al., 2013; Leveque et al., 2016; Zendel et al., 2015; see Peretz, 2016 for review).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the functional consequence of connectivity differences, supported by citations.

claim: Congenital amusia is believed to be innate.
source: While congenital amusia is believed to be innate, there is evidence that recovery is possible through training (Whiteford and Oxenham, 2018).
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field based on established knowledge.

claim: There is evidence that recovery from congenital amusia is possible through training.
source: While congenital amusia is believed to be innate, there is evidence that recovery is possible through training (Whiteford and Oxenham, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a training study.

claim: Pitch is important for cueing categories in spoken language.
source: Although pitch is usually associated with music, it is also important for cueing categories in spoken language (de Pijper and Sanderman, 1994; Streeter, 1978) and conveying emotion in speech (Frick, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to speech prosody research.

claim: Pitch is important for conveying emotion in speech.
source: Although pitch is usually associated with music, it is also important for cueing categories in spoken language (de Pijper and Sanderman, 1994; Streeter, 1978) and conveying emotion in speech (Frick, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on emotional prosody.

claim: In highly controlled laboratory tasks where speech perception judgments must be made based on pitch alone, only minor deficits have been observed in amusia.
source: In highly controlled laboratory tasks in which speech perception judgments must be made based on pitch alone, only minor deficits have been observed in amusia (Liu et al., 2015a; Patel et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: People with amusia rarely report any difficulties in naturalistic speech perception contexts.
source: In naturalistic speech perception contexts, people with amusia rarely report any difficulties (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on self-reported difficulties.

claim: In natural speech, pitch variation tends to co-occur with variation in other acoustic dimensions, such as duration and amplitude.
source: This may be because, in natural speech, pitch variation tends to co-occur with variation in other acoustic dimensions, such as duration and amplitude.
evidence: This is a statement about the acoustic properties of natural speech based on established knowledge in speech science.

claim: English-speaking individuals with amusia tend to rely less on pitch than non-amusic controls when multiple redundant cues are available.
source: Our lab has shown that in such cases where multiple redundant cues are available, English-speaking individuals with amusia tend to rely less on pitch than non-amusic controls, suggesting they may calibrate their perception by down-weighting the cues that are less reliable for them (Jasmin et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous behavioral work from the authors' lab.

claim: Individuals with amusia may calibrate their perception by down-weighting the cues that are less reliable for them.
source: Our lab has shown that in such cases where multiple redundant cues are available, English-speaking individuals with amusia tend to rely less on pitch than non-amusic controls, suggesting they may calibrate their perception by down-weighting the cues that are less reliable for them (Jasmin et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of behavioral findings, representing a theoretical claim about perceptual strategy.

claim: Individuals with amusia can recognize emotions in spoken sentences.
source: As for emotional prosody in speech, individuals with amusia can recognize emotions in spoken sentences, but not in short samples such as isolated vowels (Pralus et al., 2019), or when speech has been filtered to remove high-frequency non-pitch cues (Lolli et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on emotional prosody recognition.

claim: Individuals with amusia cannot recognize emotions in short samples such as isolated vowels.
source: As for emotional prosody in speech, individuals with amusia can recognize emotions in spoken sentences, but not in short samples such as isolated vowels (Pralus et al., 2019), or when speech has been filtered to remove high-frequency non-pitch cues (Lolli et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on emotional prosody perception.

claim: Individuals with amusia cannot recognize emotions when speech has been filtered to remove high-frequency non-pitch cues.
source: As for emotional prosody in speech, individuals with amusia can recognize emotions in spoken sentences, but not in short samples such as isolated vowels (Pralus et al., 2019), or when speech has been filtered to remove high-frequency non-pitch cues (Lolli et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a filtered speech study.

claim: It is unknown how decreased reliance on a particular acoustic cue during speech perception is reflected in the brain.
source: It is unknown how decreased reliance on a particular acoustic cue during speech perception (such as pitch cues in amusia) is reflected in the brain.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: In the 'weighted connections' model of multisensory integration, the relative reliability of the modalities involved with perception of a stimulus is related to differential connectivity strength.
source: In this model, the relative reliability of the modalities involved with perception of a stimulus is related to differential connectivity strength (Beauchamp et al., 2010; Rohe and Noppeney, 2018).
evidence: This describes a theoretical model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: When visual information is degraded, the connection strength between lateral occipital cortex and intraparietal sulcus decreases.
source: More concretely, when visual information is degraded, the connection strength between lateral occipital cortex (a visual area) and intraparietal sulcus (a multimodal area) decreases, and when tactile perception is made noisier, connection strength between secondary somatosensory cortex and intraparietal sulcus becomes weaker (Beauchamp et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited multisensory integration study.

claim: When tactile perception is made noisier, connection strength between secondary somatosensory cortex and intraparietal sulcus becomes weaker.
source: More concretely, when visual information is degraded, the connection strength between lateral occipital cortex (a visual area) and intraparietal sulcus (a multimodal area) decreases, and when tactile perception is made noisier, connection strength between secondary somatosensory cortex and intraparietal sulcus becomes weaker (Beauchamp et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited multisensory integration study.

claim: Connection strength between auditory cortex and the STS is weaker when noise has been introduced to the auditory speech.
source: Similarly, effective connectivity between the (multimodal) superior temporal sulcus (STS) and visual and auditory areas has shown similar modulations during processing of audiovisual speech: connection strength between auditory cortex and the STS is weaker when noise has been introduced to the auditory speech, and conversely connection strength between visual cortex and STS is weaker if visual noise is introduced (Nath and Beauchamp, 2011).
evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited audiovisual speech study.

claim: Connection strength between visual cortex and STS is weaker if visual noise is introduced.
source: Similarly, effective connectivity between the (multimodal) superior temporal sulcus (STS) and visual and auditory areas has shown similar modulations during processing of audiovisual speech: connection strength between auditory cortex and the STS is weaker when noise has been introduced to the auditory speech, and conversely connection strength between visual cortex and STS is weaker if visual noise is introduced (Nath and Beauchamp, 2011).
evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited audiovisual speech study.

claim: The acoustic speech signal carries multiple co-occurring acoustic dimensions (e.g. voice pitch, duration, and amplitude), which often provide redundant cues to disambiguate a linguistic category.
source: As mentioned, the acoustic speech signal carries multiple co-occurring acoustic dimensions (e.g. roughly described as voice pitch, duration, and amplitude), which often provide redundant cues to disambiguate a linguistic category (Patel, 2014; Winter, 2014; Jasmin et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is a statement about speech acoustics supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Individuals with typical pitch perception have learned through a lifetime of experience with speech acoustics that vocal pitch is a useful and reliable cue.
source: Individuals with typical pitch perception have learned through a lifetime of experience with speech acoustics that vocal pitch is a useful and reliable cue.
evidence: This is an inference about perceptual learning in typical individuals based on general principles.

claim: Individuals with amusia would have learned that, for them, pitch is not a reliable cue for processing spoken language.
source: By contrast, individuals with amusia, who have unreliable perception of and memory for pitch (analogous to the 'noise' introduced in the multisensory integration studies cited above), would have learned that, for them, pitch is not a reliable cue for processing spoken language.
evidence: This is an inference about perceptual learning in individuals with amusia based on their pitch processing difficulties.

claim: Amusics may exhibit decreased connectivity between language regions and pitch-related areas during speech processing.
source: Thus, by analogy to the multisensory weighting results described above, we hypothesize that amusics may exhibit decreased connectivity between language regions and pitch-related areas during speech processing.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, based on inference from multisensory integration literature.

claim: The neural foundations of perceptual weighting in speech have not been investigated in atypical individuals.
source: The neural foundations of perceptual weighting in speech have thus far not been investigated in atypical individuals.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Only one previous functional neuroimaging study has examined the neural processing of spoken material in people with amusia.
source: Indeed, only one previous functional neuroimaging study has examined the neural processing of spoken material in people with amusia.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on knowledge of previous studies.

claim: In the Albouy et al. 2019 study, no group differences were detected in task-related activation or functional connectivity during processing of speech.
source: In this study, no group differences were detected in task-related activation or functional connectivity during processing of speech (whereas group differences were observed during processing of tones; Albouy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: In the Albouy et al. 2019 study, group differences were observed during processing of tones.
source: In this study, no group differences were detected in task-related activation or functional connectivity during processing of speech (whereas group differences were observed during processing of tones; Albouy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: The connectivity analyses in the Albouy et al. 2019 study focused on the silent retention interval in a task in which participants needed to maintain phonemic and not pitch-related information in memory.
source: However, the connectivity analyses in this study focused on the silent retention interval in a task in which participants needed to maintain phonemic and not pitch-related information in memory; the analyses also used broader bilateral ROIs within networks associated with language processing.
evidence: This describes methodological details of a cited previous study.

claim: The Albouy et al. 2019 study used broader bilateral ROIs within networks associated with language processing.
source: However, the connectivity analyses in this study focused on the silent retention interval in a task in which participants needed to maintain phonemic and not pitch-related information in memory; the analyses also used broader bilateral ROIs within networks associated with language processing.
evidence: This describes methodological details of a cited previous study.

claim: It remains an open question how functional connectivity in amusic and non-amusic participants may differ during speech encoding in pitch-related language tasks within regions of interest selected with a whole-brain data-driven approach.
source: It remains an open question how functional connectivity in amusic and non-amusic participants may differ during speech encoding in pitch-related language tasks within regions of interest selected with a whole-brain data-driven approach.
evidence: This identifies the specific research question addressed by the current study.

claim: The study scanned 15 individuals with amusia and 15 controls using functional magnetic resonance imaging.
source: To determine whether the relative reliability of auditory dimensions in speech perception is reflected in functional connectivity, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to scan 15 individuals with amusia and 15 controls.
evidence: This describes the sample size and methodology of the current study.

claim: Participants matched spoken sentences with visually presented ones on the basis of the position of intonational phrase boundaries.
source: Participants matched spoken sentences with visually presented ones on the basis of the position of intonational phrase boundaries.
evidence: This describes the experimental task used in the study.

claim: In the Pitch-Informative condition, only pitch cues could be used to make the judgment.
source: These intonation changes were conveyed differently, in three conditions: Pitch-Informative (where only pitch cues could be used to make the judgment), Duration-Informative (where only duration cues could be used) or Both-Informative (both pitch and duration cues could be used; Jasmin et al., 2020a; Jasmin et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and conditions.

claim: In the Duration-Informative condition, only duration cues could be used to make the judgment.
source: These intonation changes were conveyed differently, in three conditions: Pitch-Informative (where only pitch cues could be used to make the judgment), Duration-Informative (where only duration cues could be used) or Both-Informative (both pitch and duration cues could be used; Jasmin et al., 2020a; Jasmin et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and conditions.

claim: In the Both-Informative condition, both pitch and duration cues could be used.
source: These intonation changes were conveyed differently, in three conditions: Pitch-Informative (where only pitch cues could be used to make the judgment), Duration-Informative (where only duration cues could be used) or Both-Informative (both pitch and duration cues could be used; Jasmin et al., 2020a; Jasmin et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and conditions.

claim: Task performance was matched between the groups.
source: Crucially, task performance was matched between the groups (based on prior behavioural testing; Jasmin et al., 2020a), ensuring that any neural differences did not simply represent an inability to perform the task.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design based on prior behavioral data.

claim: Functional connectivity between regions identified in the speech task was compared to functional connectivity calculated from different scanning runs with a passive listening task.
source: Finally, functional connectivity between these areas was analyzed with respect to prosodic cue weights obtained outside the scanner, and also compared to functional connectivity calculated from different scanning runs with a passive listening task.
evidence: This describes an additional analysis performed in the study.

claim: Overall, proportion correct across amusia and control groups was matched.
source: Overall, proportion correct across amusia and control groups was matched (main effect of Group, F(1,84) = 0.16, p=0.69, interaction of Group by Condition, F(2,84) = 0.374, p=0.96).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data collected in the scanner.

claim: The lack of interaction between Group and Condition was predicted based on previous results obtained from a similar paradigm using out-of-scanner data from the same participants.
source: This lack of interaction was predicted based on previous results obtained from a similar paradigm using out-of-scanner data but from the same participants (Jasmin et al., 2020a).
evidence: This relates the current findings to previous behavioral work.

claim: There was a main effect of condition on performance.
source: There was a main effect of condition (F(2,84) = 3.32, p=0.04).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: Performance in the Both-Informative condition was more accurate than in the Pitch-Informative condition.
source: Follow-up post-hoc testing indicated that performance in the Both-Informative condition (with pitch and duration cues simultaneously present) was more accurate than either Pitch-Informative (t(84) = 2.31, p=0.023) or Duration-Informative (t(84) = 2.15, p=0.03), a result that was also predicted and which replicates the behavioral findings in Jasmin et al., 2020a.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc testing of the behavioral data.

claim: Performance in the Both-Informative condition was more accurate than in the Duration-Informative condition.
source: Follow-up post-hoc testing indicated that performance in the Both-Informative condition (with pitch and duration cues simultaneously present) was more accurate than either Pitch-Informative (t(84) = 2.31, p=0.023) or Duration-Informative (t(84) = 2.15, p=0.03), a result that was also predicted and which replicates the behavioral findings in Jasmin et al., 2020a.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc testing of the behavioral data.

claim: The finding that performance in the Both-Informative condition was more accurate replicates the behavioral findings in Jasmin et al., 2020a.
source: Follow-up post-hoc testing indicated that performance in the Both-Informative condition (with pitch and duration cues simultaneously present) was more accurate than either Pitch-Informative (t(84) = 2.31, p=0.023) or Duration-Informative (t(84) = 2.15, p=0.03), a result that was also predicted and which replicates the behavioral findings in Jasmin et al., 2020a.
evidence: This relates the current findings to previous work.

claim: Comparing whole-brain connectedness values by group revealed four significant locations that showed greater whole-brain connectedness for the control than for the amusia group.
source: Comparing whole-brain connectedness values by group (Amusia vs. Controls) revealed four significant locations (where z of peak vertices > 4.61, FDR-corrected p<0.05) that showed greater whole-brain connectedness for the control than for the amusia group (see Figure 3, yellow crosses).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the neuroimaging analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: All group differences in whole-brain connectedness were located in the inferior frontal cortex.
source: All group differences were located in the inferior frontal cortex: two left hemisphere vertices (inferior frontal gyrus p. triangularis and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) and two right hemisphere vertices (inferior frontal gyrus p. triangularis and p. orbitalis).
evidence: This describes the anatomical locations of the connectivity differences found in the analysis.

claim: There were no areas where whole-brain connectedness differed by Condition.
source: There were no areas where whole-brain connectedness differed by Condition, or showed an interaction of Group and Condition.
evidence: This is a null result from the neuroimaging analysis.

claim: There were no areas where whole-brain connectedness showed an interaction of Group and Condition.
source: There were no areas where whole-brain connectedness differed by Condition, or showed an interaction of Group and Condition.
evidence: This is a null result from the neuroimaging analysis.

claim: Amusic participants' left inferior frontal gyrus seed region showed particularly notable decreases in connectivity with the right posterior superior temporal and inferior parietal cortex.
source: Relative to control participants, amusic participants' left inferior frontal gyrus seed region showed particularly notable decreases in connectivity with the right posterior superior temporal and inferior parietal cortex, as well as with the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Amusic participants' left inferior frontal gyrus seed region showed particularly notable decreases in connectivity with the right posterior superior temporal sulcus.
source: Relative to control participants, amusic participants' left inferior frontal gyrus seed region showed particularly notable decreases in connectivity with the right posterior superior temporal and inferior parietal cortex, as well as with the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: There was weaker connectivity between left inferior frontal gyrus and the right nucleus accumbens in the amusia group.
source: Analysis of subcortical connectivity indicated that there was also weaker connectivity with the right nucleus accumbens (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the subcortical connectivity analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the mid portions of the right superior temporal gyrus.
source: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the mid portions of the right superior temporal gyrus, posterior part of the right middle temporal gyrus extending into the inferior bank of the superior temporal sulcus, and the right anterior insula (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the posterior part of the right middle temporal gyrus extending into the inferior bank of the superior temporal sulcus.
source: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the mid portions of the right superior temporal gyrus, posterior part of the right middle temporal gyrus extending into the inferior bank of the superior temporal sulcus, and the right anterior insula (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the right anterior insula.
source: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the mid portions of the right superior temporal gyrus, posterior part of the right middle temporal gyrus extending into the inferior bank of the superior temporal sulcus, and the right anterior insula (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Several subcortical structures showed significantly reduced connectivity with the left DLPFC seed in amusics, including bilateral caudate nucleus and putamen, bilateral pallidum, bilateral cerebellum, and bilateral thalamus.
source: Several subcortical structures - bilateral caudate nucleus and putamen, bilateral pallidum, bilateral cerebellum, and bilateral thalamus - also showed significantly reduced (FDR-corrected) connectivity with the seed in amusics (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the subcortical connectivity analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: The right pars triangularis seed showed Control > Amusic connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: The right pars triangularis seed showed Control > Amusic connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The right pars triangularis seed showed Control > Amusic connectivity with left posterior superior temporal gyrus.
source: The right pars triangularis seed showed Control > Amusic connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The right pars triangularis seed showed decreased connectivity with left nucleus accumbens in the amusia group.
source: It also showed decreased connectivity with left nucleus accumbens.
evidence: This is a finding from the subcortical connectivity analysis.

claim: Right pars orbitalis showed decreased connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in the amusia group.
source: Right pars orbitalis showed decreased connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Right pars orbitalis showed decreased connectivity with the left thalamus in the amusia group.
source: There was also decreased connectivity with the left thalamus (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the subcortical connectivity analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Normalized cue weights were correlated with L-DLPFC <=> R insula connectivity (Spearman R = 0.78, p=0.000037).
source: Across this subset of participants, normalized cue weights were correlated with L-DLPFC <=> R insula connectivity (Spearman R = 0.78, p=0.000037), and L-DLPFC <=> R auditory cortex connectivity (Spearman R = 0.75, p=0.000154; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Normalized cue weights were correlated with L-DLPFC <=> R auditory cortex connectivity (Spearman R = 0.75, p=0.000154).
source: Across this subset of participants, normalized cue weights were correlated with L-DLPFC <=> R insula connectivity (Spearman R = 0.78, p=0.000037), and L-DLPFC <=> R auditory cortex connectivity (Spearman R = 0.75, p=0.000154; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Participants who relied least on pitch information to process speech had the weakest functional connectivity between L-DLPFC and right insula/auditory cortex.
source: This indicated that participants who relied least on pitch information to process speech had the weakest functional connectivity between these areas, while those who relied most on pitch had the strongest.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results.

claim: Participants who relied most on pitch had the strongest functional connectivity between L-DLPFC and right insula/auditory cortex.
source: This indicated that participants who relied least on pitch information to process speech had the weakest functional connectivity between these areas, while those who relied most on pitch had the strongest.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results.

claim: During speech perception, amusic subjects showed reduced functional connectivity between left frontal and right insula/auditory ROIs relative to controls.
source: Whereas during speech perception amusic subjects showed reduced functional connectivity between left frontal and right insula/auditory ROIs relative to controls (p=0.0001 for both ROIs; in line with the whole-brain imaging analyses), this pattern did not hold during passive listening to tones (Amusia vs Control connectivity, p=0.29, Group (Amusic, Control) by Task (Speech Perception, Passive Tone Listening) interaction p=0.045 for the insula ROI; Amusia vs Control p=0.30, Group by Task interaction p=0.035 for the auditory cortex ROI - see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison between speech and tone listening tasks, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The pattern of reduced connectivity between left frontal and right insula/auditory ROIs in amusics did not hold during passive listening to tones.
source: Whereas during speech perception amusic subjects showed reduced functional connectivity between left frontal and right insula/auditory ROIs relative to controls (p=0.0001 for both ROIs; in line with the whole-brain imaging analyses), this pattern did not hold during passive listening to tones (Amusia vs Control connectivity, p=0.29, Group (Amusic, Control) by Task (Speech Perception, Passive Tone Listening) interaction p=0.045 for the insula ROI; Amusia vs Control p=0.30, Group by Task interaction p=0.035 for the auditory cortex ROI - see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison between speech and tone listening tasks, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The Group by Task interactions suggest that the neural connectivity results are specifically linked to speech perception, rather than reflecting an overall connectivity difference between groups regardless of task state.
source: These interactions suggest that our neural connectivity results are specifically linked to speech perception, rather than reflecting an overall connectivity difference between groups regardless of task state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction effects from the task comparison.

claim: No significant differences in activation levels were detected for the main effects of group and condition, nor the interaction of those factors.
source: No significant differences were detected for the main effects of group and condition, nor the interaction of those factors.
evidence: This is a null result from the activation analysis.

claim: Individuals with amusia exhibited decreased functional connectivity between left frontal areas and right hemisphere pitch-related regions.
source: We found that individuals with amusia, who have been previously shown to rely less on pitch than controls to process spoken language (Jasmin et al., 2020a), exhibited decreased functional connectivity between left frontal areas and right hemisphere pitch-related regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the neuroimaging analysis.

claim: The amusic group exhibited decreased functional connectivity with several sites in frontal, temporal and occipital cortex.
source: Using a data-driven approach, we identified four regions in left and right inferior frontal cortex for which the amusic group exhibited decreased functional connectivity with several other sites in frontal, temporal and occipital cortex.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from the whole-brain connectivity analysis.

claim: The most prominent result was decreased connectivity between left frontal regions classically implicated in language processing (left IFG and DLPFC) and right hemisphere regions in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, and anterior insula.
source: The most prominent of these results was decreased connectivity between left frontal regions classically implicated in language processing (left IFG and DLPFC) and right hemisphere regions —in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, and anterior insula—that have been implicated in pitch processing (Lee et al., 2011; Garcea et al., 2017; Warren et al., 2003; Hohmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This summarizes the most prominent finding and relates it to the literature on pitch processing regions.

claim: Right hemisphere regions in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, and anterior insula have been implicated in pitch processing.
source: The most prominent of these results was decreased connectivity between left frontal regions classically implicated in language processing (left IFG and DLPFC) and right hemisphere regions —in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, and anterior insula—that have been implicated in pitch processing (Lee et al., 2011; Garcea et al., 2017; Warren et al., 2003; Hohmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the functional role of brain regions based on citations to the literature.

claim: The decreased connectivity between right hemisphere pitch and left hemisphere frontal cortices may relate to the unreliability of the amusics' perception of and memory for pitch.
source: We suggest that this decreased connectivity between right hemisphere pitch and left hemisphere frontal cortices may relate to the unreliability of the amusics' perception of and memory for pitch.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to perceptual reliability.

claim: The decreased connectivity pattern is similar to the 'weighted connections' model of multisensory integration, where a more (or less) reliable modality is given a stronger (or weaker) weight.
source: This is similar to the 'weighted connections' model of multisensory integration, where a more (or less) reliable modality is given a stronger (or weaker) weight (Beauchamp et al., 2010).
evidence: This draws an analogy between the current findings and a theoretical model from the literature.

claim: Congenital amusia is often described as a disorder related to structural and functional connectivity within the right hemisphere, particularly between right inferior frontal cortices and right posterior temporal cortex.
source: Congenital amusia is often described as a disorder related to structural and functional connectivity within the right hemisphere, particularly between right inferior frontal cortices and right posterior temporal cortex (see Peretz, 2016 for review).
evidence: This summarizes the prevailing view in the literature, supported by citation to a review.

claim: Right inferior frontal cortex exhibited strongly decreased functional connectivity in the amusia group.
source: Consistent with this proposal, we found in the present study that right inferior frontal cortex exhibited strongly decreased functional connectivity in the amusia group, and follow-up seed testing revealed that right auditory areas were involved as well.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study that is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Sites in left frontal cortex also showed large decreases in connectivity in amusia, most prominently with right hemisphere auditory areas.
source: However, we also found that sites in left frontal cortex also showed large decreases in connectivity in amusia, also most prominently with right hemisphere auditory areas.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study that extends beyond previous literature.

claim: The results are consistent with an account that right hemisphere auditory areas are not only abnormally connected to right frontal areas but are less integrated with frontal left hemisphere regions when processing speech and language.
source: Our results are consistent with an account that right hemisphere auditory areas are not only abnormally connected to right frontal areas (as observed during tonal tasks) but are less integrated with frontal left hemisphere regions when processing speech and language.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings that extends the prevailing theoretical account.

claim: The null results for group differences in activation during speech processing are consistent with prior reports that amusics and controls do not differ in pitch representations within sensory regions.
source: Our null results for group differences in activation during speech processing are consistent with prior reports that amusics and controls do not differ in pitch representations within sensory regions.
evidence: This relates the null activation findings to previous literature.

claim: The extent of pitch-responsive regions within auditory cortex has been shown to be similar in participants with amusia and controls.
source: For example, the extent of pitch-responsive regions within auditory cortex has been shown to be similar in participants with amusia and controls (Norman-Haignere et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citation.

claim: Brainstem encoding of pitch in speech and musical stimuli is unimpaired in individuals with amusia.
source: Brainstem encoding of pitch in speech and musical stimuli is similarly unimpaired in individuals with amusia (Liu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citation.

claim: In oddball EEG paradigms, amusics show similar pre-attentive mismatch negativity responses to small pitch deviants.
source: Moreover, in oddball EEG paradigms, amusics show similar pre-attentive mismatch negativity responses to small pitch deviants, but impaired attention-dependent P300 responses (Moreau et al., 2009; Peretz et al., 2009; Mignault Goulet et al., 2012; Moreau et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: In oddball EEG paradigms, amusics show impaired attention-dependent P300 responses to pitch deviants.
source: Moreover, in oddball EEG paradigms, amusics show similar pre-attentive mismatch negativity responses to small pitch deviants, but impaired attention-dependent P300 responses (Moreau et al., 2009; Peretz et al., 2009; Mignault Goulet et al., 2012; Moreau et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Amusics show intact non-volitional behavioral responses (unconscious pitch shifts) when presented with pitch-altered feedback of their own voice.
source: These findings, along with the fact that amusics show intact non-volitional behavioral responses (unconscious pitch shifts) when presented with pitch-altered feedback of their own voice (Hutchins and Peretz, 2012), have been interpreted as evidence that amusia is a disorder of pitch awareness rather than one of low-level pitch processing (Peretz et al., 2009), with differences in structural connectivity as one possible foundation of this putative impaired pitch awareness (Hyde et al., 2006; Loui et al., 2009; but see Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citation.

claim: The findings have been interpreted as evidence that amusia is a disorder of pitch awareness rather than one of low-level pitch processing.
source: These findings, along with the fact that amusics show intact non-volitional behavioral responses (unconscious pitch shifts) when presented with pitch-altered feedback of their own voice (Hutchins and Peretz, 2012), have been interpreted as evidence that amusia is a disorder of pitch awareness rather than one of low-level pitch processing (Peretz et al., 2009), with differences in structural connectivity as one possible foundation of this putative impaired pitch awareness (Hyde et al., 2006; Loui et al., 2009; but see Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a theoretical interpretation from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Differences in structural connectivity have been proposed as one possible foundation of impaired pitch awareness in amusia.
source: These findings, along with the fact that amusics show intact non-volitional behavioral responses (unconscious pitch shifts) when presented with pitch-altered feedback of their own voice (Hutchins and Peretz, 2012), have been interpreted as evidence that amusia is a disorder of pitch awareness rather than one of low-level pitch processing (Peretz et al., 2009), with differences in structural connectivity as one possible foundation of this putative impaired pitch awareness (Hyde et al., 2006; Loui et al., 2009; but see Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a theoretical proposal from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Down-weighting of pitch information during perceptual categorization in both speech and music is adaptive in amusics, inasmuch as they have learned that pitch is an unreliable source of evidence relative to other perceptual dimensions.
source: Our interpretation of differences in functional connectivity between amusics and controls diverges somewhat from these previous approaches: we argue that down-weighting of pitch information during perceptual categorization in both speech and music is adaptive, inasmuch as amusics have learned that pitch is an unreliable source of evidence relative to other perceptual dimensions.
evidence: This is the authors' theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: The fundamental deficit in amusia may not be increased perceptual noise or decreased pitch awareness but difficulties with retention of pitch information in memory.
source: The evidence above suggesting that encoding of pitch in the brainstem and auditory cortex and pre-attentive responses to pitch changes are unaffected in amusia can be interpreted as suggesting that the fundamental deficit in amusia may not be increased perceptual noise or decreased pitch awareness but difficulties with retention of pitch information in memory (see Tillmann et al., 2016 for review).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation to a review.

claim: The task arguably taxed working memory resources.
source: Our task arguably taxed working memory resources: in a similar paradigm performed by the same participants in quiet listening conditions (Jasmin et al., 2020a), the mean reaction time measured from the end of the second auditory stimulus was 1.64 s, indicating that participants needed some time to compare both auditory presentations and make their judgments.
evidence: This is an inference about the cognitive demands of the task based on reaction time data from a previous study.

claim: Amusics have difficulty with pitch sequence processing tasks even when discrimination thresholds are accounted for.
source: This interpretation is consistent with evidence suggesting that amusics have difficulty with pitch sequence processing tasks even when discrimination thresholds are accounted for (Tillmann et al., 2009), as well as the finding that delaying the time interval between standard and comparison tones exacerbates pitch discrimination impairment in individuals with amusia (Williamson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citation.

claim: Delaying the time interval between standard and comparison tones exacerbates pitch discrimination impairment in individuals with amusia.
source: This interpretation is consistent with evidence suggesting that amusics have difficulty with pitch sequence processing tasks even when discrimination thresholds are accounted for (Tillmann et al., 2009), as well as the finding that delaying the time interval between standard and comparison tones exacerbates pitch discrimination impairment in individuals with amusia (Williamson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citation.

claim: The pitch awareness account of amusia cannot explain the finding that pitch cues are downweighted only during longer-scale suprasegmental speech perception while pitch weighting is not different between amusics and controls during shorter-scale segmental speech perception.
source: Moreover, the pitch awareness account of amusia cannot explain the Jasmin et al., 2020a finding that pitch cues are downweighted only during longer-scale suprasegmental speech perception, while pitch weighting is not different between amusics and controls during shorter-scale segmental speech perception, despite pitch cues being arguably more subtle in the segmental condition.
evidence: This is a logical argument against an alternative theoretical account based on previous findings.

claim: The finding that pitch cues are downweighted only during suprasegmental but not segmental speech perception can be explained by the pitch memory account, as the suprasegmental task requires detection of and memory for pitch patterns within a complex sequence, while the segmental task does not.
source: However, this finding can be explained by the pitch memory account, as the suprasegmental task requires detection of and memory for pitch patterns within a complex sequence, while the segmental task does not.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation of previous findings based on the authors' proposed account.

claim: An account of amusia which suggests that the disorder primarily stems from differences in structural connectivity cannot account for the finding that functional connectivity patterns do not differ between amusics and controls during a verbal memory task.
source: Furthermore, an account of amusia which suggests that the disorder primarily stems from differences in structural connectivity cannot account for the recent finding that functional connectivity patterns do not differ between amusics and controls during a verbal memory task (Albouy et al., 2019), as well as our finding that amusics and controls show similar functional connectivity patterns during passive listening to tone sequences.
evidence: This is a logical argument against an alternative theoretical account based on previous and current findings.

claim: Amusics and controls show similar functional connectivity patterns during passive listening to tone sequences.
source: Furthermore, an account of amusia which suggests that the disorder primarily stems from differences in structural connectivity cannot account for the recent finding that functional connectivity patterns do not differ between amusics and controls during a verbal memory task (Albouy et al., 2019), as well as our finding that amusics and controls show similar functional connectivity patterns during passive listening to tone sequences.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's comparison task.

claim: Amusics neglect pitch because they have implicitly learned that their memory for pitch is unreliable.
source: We suggest, therefore, that amusics neglect pitch because they have implicitly learned that their memory for pitch is unreliable, and that this down-weighting of pitch is reflected in decreased functional connectivity between right auditory areas and downstream task-relevant areas which integrate information from perceptual regions.
evidence: This is the authors' theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: Down-weighting of pitch in amusics is reflected in decreased functional connectivity between right auditory areas and downstream task-relevant areas which integrate information from perceptual regions.
source: We suggest, therefore, that amusics neglect pitch because they have implicitly learned that their memory for pitch is unreliable, and that this down-weighting of pitch is reflected in decreased functional connectivity between right auditory areas and downstream task-relevant areas which integrate information from perceptual regions.
evidence: This is the authors' theoretical interpretation linking behavior to neural findings.

claim: A previous fMRI study on amusia detected group differences in functional connectivity during passive listening to tones.
source: We note that a previous fMRI study on amusia detected group differences in functional connectivity during passive listening to tones.
evidence: This references findings from previous literature.

claim: The Hyde et al. 2011 study used task-defined seed voxels in bilateral auditory cortex and found, in the amusia group, increased connectivity between left and right auditory cortex.
source: That study used task-defined seed voxels in bilateral auditory cortex and found, in the amusia group, increased connectivity between left and right auditory cortex, but decreased connectivity between right auditory cortex and right inferior frontal gyrus (Hyde et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: The Hyde et al. 2011 study found decreased connectivity between right auditory cortex and right inferior frontal gyrus in the amusia group.
source: That study used task-defined seed voxels in bilateral auditory cortex and found, in the amusia group, increased connectivity between left and right auditory cortex, but decreased connectivity between right auditory cortex and right inferior frontal gyrus (Hyde et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: The present study does not necessarily clash with the Hyde et al. 2011 findings, as different seed ROIs were used selected with a different procedure.
source: The present study does not necessarily clash with these findings, as we used different seed ROIs selected with a different procedure.
evidence: This is a statement reconciling the current findings with previous literature based on methodological differences.

claim: No differences in functional connectivity between conditions were observed in the speech task.
source: We did not observe any differences in functional connectivity between conditions in our speech task.
evidence: This is a null result from the neuroimaging analysis.

claim: The functional imaging protocol was timed to capture the peak in the BOLD signal corresponding to the presentation of the second auditory stimulus.
source: This may be because our functional imaging protocol was timed to capture the peak in the BOLD signal corresponding to the presentation of the second auditory stimulus.
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the study.

claim: Participants never knew (even implicitly) which acoustic dimension might be useful on any given trial until after they had heard both spoken sentences.
source: Participants never knew (even implicitly) which acoustic dimension might be useful on any given trial until after they had heard both spoken sentences and needed to compare them to make their response.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental design.

claim: Pitch fluctuations in the stimuli were above participants' thresholds, even in the Duration-Informative condition.
source: Furthermore, pitch fluctuations in the stimuli were above participants' thresholds , even in the Duration-Informative condition (where the standard deviation of F0 over each spoken utterance was, on average, 2.7 semitones), and so it is unsurprising that functional connectivity did not change on a trial-by-trial basis, and instead the same 'neural strategy' was employed to process speech regardless of the trial type.
evidence: This describes an acoustic property of the stimuli.

claim: The same 'neural strategy' was employed to process speech regardless of the trial type.
source: Furthermore, pitch fluctuations in the stimuli were above participants' thresholds , even in the Duration-Informative condition (where the standard deviation of F0 over each spoken utterance was, on average, 2.7 semitones), and so it is unsurprising that functional connectivity did not change on a trial-by-trial basis, and instead the same 'neural strategy' was employed to process speech regardless of the trial type.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the null condition effects.

claim: In the multimodal integration studies, reliability of two different sensory modalities was manipulated experimentally by severely degrading input channels with noise, resulting in changes in connectivity.
source: In the multimodal integration studies mentioned above (Beauchamp et al., 2010; Nath and Beauchamp, 2011), reliability of two different sensory modalities was manipulated experimentally by severely degrading input channels with noise, resulting in changes in connectivity.
evidence: This describes methods and findings from cited previous studies.

claim: Behavioral work has indicated that when fundamental frequency (pitch) or durational aspects of speech are manipulated to be unreliable cues, categorization behavior shifts such that participants place less relative weight on the dimension that has been made less reliable.
source: Indeed, behavioral work has indicated that when fundamental frequency (pitch) or durational aspects of speech are manipulated to be unreliable cues, categorization behavior shifts such that participants place less relative weight on the dimension that has been made less reliable (Holt and Lotto, 2010).
evidence: This describes findings from cited behavioral research.

claim: Tone language speakers are known to have fine-grained pitch perception abilities.
source: Certain groups, such as tone language speakers, are known to have fine-grained pitch perception abilities, and tend to place greater weight on pitch even when processing speech from a second, non-tonal language that they have learned (e.g. English; Yu and Andruski, 2010; Zhang and Francis, 2010, Zhang et al., 2008; Qin et al., 2017; Jasmin et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is a statement about tone language speakers supported by citations.

claim: Tone language speakers tend to place greater weight on pitch even when processing speech from a second, non-tonal language that they have learned.
source: Certain groups, such as tone language speakers, are known to have fine-grained pitch perception abilities, and tend to place greater weight on pitch even when processing speech from a second, non-tonal language that they have learned (e.g. English; Yu and Andruski, 2010; Zhang and Francis, 2010, Zhang et al., 2008; Qin et al., 2017; Jasmin et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is a claim about tone language speakers' perceptual strategies supported by citations.

claim: Given the increased reliability of their pitch perception, tone language speakers may exhibit correspondingly high connectivity strength between right hemisphere auditory regions and left hemisphere 'language regions' when pitch cues are present.
source: Given the increased reliability of their pitch perception, tone language speakers may exhibit correspondingly high connectivity strength between right hemisphere auditory regions and left hemisphere 'language regions' when pitch cues are present (more so than native non-tonal language speakers).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about neural connectivity in tone language speakers based on the current findings.

claim: Expert musicians have extensive pitch-related experience and training.
source: Expert musicians also have extensive pitch-related experience and training and could also serve as a population to examine in future work.
evidence: This is a statement about musicians based on general knowledge.

claim: The study included 15 individuals with amusia (10 F, age = 60.2 ± 9.4, range = 43–74) and 15 controls (10 F, age = 61.3 ± 10.4, range = 38–74).
source: Participants, 15 individuals with amusia (10 F, age = 60.2 ± 9.4, range = 43–74) and 15 controls (10 F, age = 61.3 ± 10.4, range = 38–74), were recruited from the UK and were native British English speakers.
evidence: This describes the participant sample characteristics.

claim: Participants were recruited from the UK and were native British English speakers.
source: Participants, 15 individuals with amusia (10 F, age = 60.2 ± 9.4, range = 43–74) and 15 controls (10 F, age = 61.3 ± 10.4, range = 38–74), were recruited from the UK and were native British English speakers.

claim: Amusia status was obtained using the Montreal Battery for the Evaluation of Amusia (MBEA).
source: Amusia status was obtained using the Montreal Battery for the Evaluation of Amusia (MBEA).
evidence: This describes the method used to classify participants.

claim: Participants with a composite MBEA score of 65 or less were classified as having amusia.
source: Participants with a composite score (summing the Scale, Contour and Interval tests scores) of 65 or less were classified as having amusia (Peretz et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the classification criterion based on a cited standardized test.

claim: The amusics defined using the MBEA had higher pitch thresholds than controls (Wilcoxon Rank Sum W = 29, p=0.001).
source: We also note that the amusics defined using the MBEA had higher pitch thresholds than controls (Wilcoxon Rank Sum W = 29, p=0.001) but did not differ from controls in tone duration discrimination (W = 129, p=0.74), speech-in-noise threshold (W = 155.5, p=0.17), or audiometric hearing thresholds (t(28) = 1.33, p=0.20; see Jasmin et al., 2020a for detailed methods for these procedures).
evidence: This is a statistical result characterizing the participant groups.

claim: Amusics did not differ from controls in tone duration discrimination.
source: We also note that the amusics defined using the MBEA had higher pitch thresholds than controls (Wilcoxon Rank Sum W = 29, p=0.001) but did not differ from controls in tone duration discrimination (W = 129, p=0.74), speech-in-noise threshold (W = 155.5, p=0.17), or audiometric hearing thresholds (t(28) = 1.33, p=0.20; see Jasmin et al., 2020a for detailed methods for these procedures).
evidence: This is a statistical result characterizing the participant groups.

claim: The stimuli were 42 compound sentences that consisted of a pre-posed subordinate clause followed by a main clause.
source: The stimuli were 42 compound sentences that consisted of a pre-posed subordinate clause followed by a main clause (see Figure 1 for an example, and Jasmin et al., 2020a, Jasmin et al., 2020b for details).
evidence: This describes the stimulus materials used in the study.

claim: Across all stimuli, F0 (vocal pitch) differences between early and late closure versions were large, with a mean of maximum difference of 7.7 semitones and range of 4.0–12.6 semitones.
source: Across all stimuli, F0 (vocal pitch) differences between early and late closure versions were large, with a mean of maximum difference of 7.7 semitones and range of 4.0–12.6 semitones.
evidence: This describes acoustic properties of the stimuli.

claim: Even the stimulus pair with the smallest pitch difference (4.0 semitones) exceeded the ~1.5 semitone pitch change detection threshold of the 'most impaired' participant in the amusia group.
source: Thus, even the stimulus pair with the smallest pitch difference (4.0 semitones) exceeded the ~1.5 semitone pitch change detection threshold of the 'most impaired' participant in the amusia group (Jasmin et al., 2020a), which increased the chances that the amusia group would not suffer from poor performance, thereby avoiding a performance-related confound with our experimental design (see Church et al., 2010 for discussion).
evidence: This relates stimulus properties to participant thresholds to justify the experimental design.

claim: Beta series correlation is a technique for examining functional connectivity and its modulation by task, using correlations in trial-by-trial responses.
source: Beta series correlation (Rissman et al., 2004) is a technique for examining functional connectivity and its modulation by task, using correlations in trial-by-trial responses.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: Beta series correlation has been shown to be more powerful than alternatives such as generalized psycho-physiological interaction (gPPI) for event-related designs.
source: It has been shown to be more powerful than alternatives such as generalized psycho-physiological interaction (gPPI) for event-related designs (Cisler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a claim about methodological advantages supported by citation.
